atoms.effect: The Attorney General may sue; the court may grant equitable and declaratory relief, monetary damages to aggrieved persons, and civil penalties of up to $55,000 for a first violation and $110,000 for any subsequent violation (as adjusted for inflation). Aggrieved persons may intervene for their own relief with costs and attorney's fees.
atoms.quote: in an amount not exceeding $55,000 for a first violation; and (B) in an amount not exceeding $110,000 for any subsequent violation.
atoms.origin: register queue batch 6, section US:50 USC 4041 (new_rule, critical)

atoms.condition: A tenant sues over an SCRA violation (US:50USC4042) or the Attorney General sues (US:50USC4041-ag-penalties).
atoms.effect: Those remedies do not limit any remedy under other law, including consequential and punitive damages (for example under state law or the lease).
atoms.quote: Nothing in section 4041 or 4042 of this title shall be construed to preclude or limit any remedy otherwise available under other law, including consequential and punitive damages.
atoms.origin: register queue batch 6, section US:50 USC 4043 (partial, major)

atoms.condition: The payee took an authorization, gave a check-conversion, returned-fee or varying-amount notice, or offered a payment plan subject to 1005.3(b)(2)-(3) or 1005.10(b), (d), (e).
atoms.effect: It keeps evidence of compliance (the signed authorization and copy sent, the notices and their dates) for at least two years from when the disclosure or action was required; once it has actual notice of an investigation or has been served in an EFTA action, it keeps the related records until final disposition.
atoms.quote: (1) Any person subject to the Act and this part shall retain evidence of compliance with the requirements imposed by the Act and this part for a period of not less than two years
atoms.origin: register queue batch 6, section US:12 CFR 1005.13 (new_rule, minor)

atoms.condition: A landlord that is a TILA creditor (US:15USC1605-plan-finance-charge) gives a payment plan for a move-out balance.
atoms.effect: TILA does not apply to a plan with a tenant that is an organization (company, partnership, LLC), to credit primarily for business or commercial purposes, or to a plan whose amount financed exceeds the statutory threshold ($50,000 as adjusted), none of which is secured by real property or the tenant's dwelling. A plan with a natural-person tenant for a residential tenancy balance under the threshold is covered.
atoms.quote: Credit transactions involving extensions of credit primarily for business, commercial, or agricultural purposes, or to government or governmental agencies or instrumentalities, or to organizations.

construction.quote: in which the total amount financed exceeds $50,000.

atoms.reasoning: 1603(1) and (3) exempt organization, business-purpose and large unsecured credit.
atoms.origin: register queue batch 6, section US:15 USC 1603 (new_rule, major)

atoms.condition: A landlord that is a TILA creditor gives a payment plan with an interest charge, and the former tenant prepays the plan in full (including after acceleration or restructuring).
atoms.effect: The landlord promptly refunds the unearned part of the interest charge (not required if under $1); for a precomputed plan longer than 61 months the refund is computed by a method at least as favorable as the actuarial method.
atoms.quote: If a consumer prepays in full the financed amount under any consumer credit transaction, the creditor shall promptly refund any unearned portion of the interest charge to the consumer.
atoms.origin: register queue batch 6, section US:15 USC 1615 (new_rule, minor)

atoms.condition: The landlord (or its manager or Handoff as payee) agreed to accept rent or a balance payment by electronic fund transfer, the tenant initiated the transfer from a consumer account, and a system malfunction prevented the transfer from being completed.
atoms.effect: The tenant's obligation for that payment is suspended until the malfunction is corrected and the transfer can be completed, so the payment is not late for that period and no late fee or default follows from it, unless the payee afterwards demanded payment by another means in a written request, from which point the tenant owes payment by that other means.
atoms.quote: the consumer’s obligation to the other person shall be suspended until the malfunction is corrected and the electronic fund transfer may be completed
atoms.origin: register queue batch 6, section US:15 USC 1693j (new_rule, major)

atoms.condition: The landlord, manager, Handoff or a collector offers a former tenant (a natural person) a payment plan for a move-out balance, which gives a right to defer payment of a debt (US:15USC1602(f)).
atoms.effect: It may not condition the plan on the tenant's repaying by preauthorized recurring electronic debits. It may offer autopay as an option, and may give a cost incentive for autopay only if a plan without autopay is also offered. A plan conditioned on autopay violates 1693k and carries 1693m liability.
atoms.quote: condition the extension of credit to a consumer on such consumer’s repayment by means of preauthorized electronic fund transfers;

construction.quote: No financial institution or other person may condition an extension of credit to a consumer on the consumer's repayment by preauthorized electronic fund transfers
provided the program with the automatic payment feature is not the only loan program offered by the creditor for the type of credit involved.
(f) “Credit” means the right granted by a financial institution to a consumer to defer payment of debt

atoms.reasoning: 1693k(1) binds any person and does not define credit; 1005.10(e)(1) extends the bar to 'other person[s]', which the 1005.2(f) definition (credit granted by a financial institution) would make surplus if read to exclude non-bank creditors. The statute controls over the regulation's definition, and 1005.3(a) applies 1005.10(e) to any person. A payment plan defers payment of a debt, which is credit under US:15USC1602(f), the definition of the same Consumer Credit Protection Act.
atoms.origin: register queue batch 6, section US:15 USC 1693k (new_rule, major)

atoms.condition: A lease, autopay form, payment-plan agreement or settlement with a tenant contains a term waiving an EFTA or Regulation E right (for example, the 10-day notice of a varying debit, or the right to stop a preauthorized debit).
atoms.effect: The waiver is void. An agreement may give the tenant greater protection, and a waiver given in settlement of a dispute or action is valid.
atoms.quote: No writing or other agreement between a consumer and any other person may contain any provision which constitutes a waiver of any right conferred or cause of action created by this subchapter.
atoms.origin: register queue batch 6, section US:15 USC 1693l (new_rule, minor)

atoms.condition: A payee knowingly and willfully fails to comply with an EFTA duty that binds it (US:12CFR1005.3(a)-payee-duties), for example debiting a tenant's account on recurring autopay without a written authorization, or gives false information it must disclose.
atoms.effect: It commits a federal crime punishable by a fine of up to $5,000, imprisonment of up to one year, or both, in addition to civil liability under US:15USC1693m-civil-liability.
atoms.quote: Whoever knowingly and willfully— (1) gives false or inaccurate information or fails to provide information which he is required to disclose by this subchapter or any regulation issued thereunder; or (2) otherwise fails to comply with any provision of this subchapter; shall be fined not more than $5,000 or imprisoned not more than one year, or both.
atoms.origin: register queue batch 6, section US:15 USC 1693n (new_rule, major)

atoms.actor: landlord; managing agent; Handoff (voucher owner and its agents)
atoms.condition: A voucher tenant tells the owner or its agent that the tenant is a victim entitled to VAWA protections or remedies (for example to explain damage, an early departure, or a perpetrator's removal).
atoms.effect: The owner may, but need not, ask in writing for documentation; the tenant chooses among the HUD certification form, a professional's signed statement, a law-enforcement, court or agency record, or (at the owner's discretion) other evidence. If none is provided within 14 business days of the written request (extendable), the VAWA protections do not limit the owner's lease remedies. Conflicting claims allow a demand for third-party documentation within 30 days. All of it, including the fact of victim status, is kept in strict confidence: no access for staff or contractors (Handoff, a collector) unless the owner specifically authorizes it for a legal need, no entry into a shared database, and no disclosure (for example to a collector, credit bureau or prospective landlord) except with the tenant's written time-limited consent, for an eviction or termination hearing, or as other law requires.
atoms.quote: shall be maintained in strict confidence by the covered housing provider.

construction.quote: within 14 business days after the date that the tenant receives a request in writing for such documentation from the covered housing provider

The covered housing provider shall not enter confidential information described in paragraph (c) of this section into any shared database or disclose such information to any other entity or individual, except to the extent that the disclosure is:

atoms.reasoning: 5.2007(a)-(b) set the documentation request and 14-business-day window; (c) the confidentiality duty and its three exceptions.
atoms.origin: register queue batch 6, section US:24 CFR 5.2007 (new_rule, major)

atoms.condition: The owner bifurcates the voucher lease to remove a household member who committed the violence, and the removed person was the eligible (voucher-holding) tenant, so the remaining tenants are not yet eligible.
atoms.effect: The bifurcation follows state and local eviction procedure. The remaining tenants get 90 calendar days from the bifurcation (extendable by the owner up to 60 more) to establish eligibility for the program or another covered program, or to find other housing, but not beyond the lease's expiration; the owner does not end their occupancy for lack of eligibility during that period. Rent for that period follows the lease and the PHA's determination of assistance (US:24CFR982.451(b)(4)).
atoms.quote: the covered housing provider shall provide to any remaining tenant or tenants that were not already eligible a period of 90 calendar days from the date of bifurcation of the lease to:

construction.quote: The 90-day calendar period also will not apply beyond the expiration of a lease, unless this is permitted by program regulations.
may extend the 90-calendar-day period in paragraph (b)(2) of this section up to an additional 60 calendar days

atoms.reasoning: 5.2009(a) authorizes bifurcation under state procedure; (b)(2) sets the 90-day period and its limits.
atoms.origin: register queue batch 6, section US:24 CFR 5.2009 (partial, major)

atoms.instrument: 24 CFR part 982 (Section 8 Tenant-Based Assistance: Housing Choice Voucher Program)
atoms.condition: Settling a tenancy assisted by a tenant-based voucher, where the lease and the HUD tenancy addendum differ (for example on the deposit, charges or termination).
atoms.effect: The tenancy addendum prevails over any other lease provision, and the tenant may enforce it against the owner; changes the owner and tenant agreed must be in writing with a copy given to the PHA at once. The settlement applies the addendum's terms first.
atoms.quote: The tenant shall have the right to enforce the tenancy addendum against the owner, and the terms of the tenancy addendum shall prevail over any other provisions of the lease.
atoms.origin: register queue batch 6, section US:24 CFR 982.308 (new_rule, major)

atoms.instrument: 24 CFR part 982 (Section 8 Tenant-Based Assistance: Housing Choice Voucher Program)
atoms.condition: The owner of a unit rented with a tenant-based voucher wants to end the tenancy during the lease term.
atoms.effect: Only for a serious or repeated lease violation (including failure to pay the tenant's rent or other amounts due under the lease), a violation of law tied to occupancy, or other good cause; during the initial term, 'other good cause' must rest on something the family did or failed to do (not a refused renewal offer, owner use, sale, renovation or a higher rent). The PHA's failure to pay its share is never a lease violation or ground to terminate. The owner must give the tenant written notice of the grounds at or before starting the eviction action (the tenancy does not end before it), give the PHA a copy of any eviction notice, and evict only by court action. Every notice under part 982 is written.
atoms.quote: During the term of the lease, the owner may not terminate the tenancy except on the following grounds:

construction.quote: The tenancy does not terminate before the owner has given this notice, and the notice must be given at or before commencement of the eviction action.
The owner may only evict the tenant from the unit by instituting a court action.
Where part 982 requires any notice to be given by the PHA, the family or the owner, the notice must be in writing.

atoms.reasoning: 982.310(a)-(f) limit grounds, require the notice of grounds and PHA copy, and require court action; 982.5 requires writing.
atoms.origin: register queue batch 6, section US:24 CFR 982.310 (new_rule, major)

atoms.instrument: 24 CFR part 982 (Section 8 Tenant-Based Assistance: Housing Choice Voucher Program)
atoms.condition: No member of a voucher family has resided in the unit for longer than the PHA's permitted absence, and in any case more than 180 consecutive days.
atoms.effect: The HAP payments, the HAP contract and the assisted lease terminate at that point, which fixes the end of the assisted tenancy for the settlement; the owner must repay the PHA any housing assistance payment received for the period after the termination, and that repayment is never charged to the family.
atoms.quote: Housing assistance payments terminate if the family is absent for longer than the maximum period permitted. The term of the HAP contract and assisted lease also terminate.

construction.quote: (The owner must reimburse the PHA for any housing assistance payment for the period after the termination.)

atoms.reasoning: 982.312(a)-(c) set the 180-day cap and the termination of the HAP contract and lease, with the owner's reimbursement duty.
atoms.origin: register queue batch 6, section US:24 CFR 982.312 (new_rule, critical)

atoms.instrument: 24 CFR part 982 (Section 8 Tenant-Based Assistance: Housing Choice Voucher Program)
atoms.condition: The PHA terminates the HAP contract because the unit is too small for the family (after notice to the family and owner) or because program funding is insufficient.
atoms.effect: For a too-small unit, the HAP contract ends at the end of the calendar month after the month the PHA notifies the owner; for insufficient funding, when the PHA terminates it. The owner receives no housing assistance payment after that date, and the family is never liable for the assistance portion (US:24CFR982.451(b)(4)); the family may move with continued assistance.
atoms.quote: The HAP contract terminates at the end of the calendar month that follows the calendar month in which the PHA gives such notice to the owner.

construction.quote: The PHA may terminate the HAP contract if the PHA determines, in accordance with HUD requirements, that funding under the consolidated ACC is insufficient to support continued assistance for families in the program.

atoms.reasoning: 982.403(b) fixes the termination date for a too-small unit; 982.454 allows funding terminations.
atoms.origin: register queue batch 6, section US:24 CFR 982.403 (new_rule, major)

atoms.instrument: 24 CFR part 982 (Section 8 Tenant-Based Assistance: Housing Choice Voucher Program)
atoms.condition: The PHA terminates the HAP contract for insufficient program funding while the family remains in the unit.
atoms.effect: No housing assistance is paid after the termination, and the lost assistance is never charged to the family (US:24CFR982.451(b)(4)); the remaining tenancy and its settlement follow the lease and state law.
atoms.quote: The PHA may terminate the HAP contract if the PHA determines, in accordance with HUD requirements, that funding under the consolidated ACC is insufficient to support continued assistance for families in the program.
atoms.origin: register queue batch 6, section US:24 CFR 982.454 (new_rule, minor)

atoms.instrument: 24 CFR part 982 (Section 8 Tenant-Based Assistance: Housing Choice Voucher Program)
atoms.condition: Part 982 requires a notice by the owner or the family (the owner's notice of grounds and copy of an eviction notice to the PHA; the family's notice of lease termination or move-out to the owner and PHA).
atoms.effect: The notice must be in writing.
atoms.quote: Where part 982 requires any notice to be given by the PHA, the family or the owner, the notice must be in writing.
atoms.origin: register queue batch 6, section US:24 CFR 982.5 (new_rule, minor)

atoms.instrument: 24 CFR part 982 (Section 8 Tenant-Based Assistance: Housing Choice Voucher Program)
atoms.condition: The owner bills a voucher tenant, during the tenancy or on the move-out account, for items other than rent (for example amenity, package, trash, or service fees, or meals and supportive services).
atoms.effect: It may not charge extra for items customarily included in rent in the locality or provided at no extra cost to unsubsidized tenants in the building, and the lease may not require payment for meals or supportive services; such charges are not owed, may not be deducted from the deposit, and non-payment of meal or service charges is not a ground to end the tenancy.
judgment_terms: customarily included in rent in the locality
atoms.quote: The owner may not charge the tenant extra amounts for items customarily included in rent in the locality, or provided at no additional cost to unsubsidized tenants in the premises.
atoms.origin: register queue batch 6, section US:24 CFR 982.510 (new_rule, major)

atoms.condition: A landlord, manager, Handoff or collector engages in a pattern or practice of discriminatory settlement or collection practices, or a denial of rights to a group raising an issue of general public importance.
atoms.effect: The Attorney General may sue; the court may order injunctive relief, monetary damages to aggrieved persons, and a civil penalty of up to $50,000 for a first violation and $100,000 for any subsequent violation (as adjusted), with attorney's fees to the prevailing party other than the United States.
atoms.quote: in an amount not exceeding $50,000, for a first violation; and (ii) in an amount not exceeding $100,000, for any subsequent violation.
atoms.origin: register queue batch 6, section US:42 USC 3614 (new_rule, critical)

atoms.condition: The landlord (or its manager) provides the tenant internet access, home security services, or a gym or fitness program under a contract or lease addendum separate from the tenancy, entered before the tenant received orders, and the servicemember tenant (or a covered spouse or dependent) receives orders to relocate for 90 days or more to a place the contract cannot serve, or a qualifying stop-movement order.
atoms.effect: The tenant may terminate that contract by written or electronic notice with a copy of the orders and the termination date; the provider gives written or electronic notice of these rights. No early termination charge may be imposed; amounts already due under the contract remain owed. Advance payments for periods after the termination date (beyond the current billing period) are refunded within 60 days. Provider-owned equipment is returned within 10 days of disconnection.
atoms.quote: For any contract terminated under this section, the service provider under the contract may not impose an early termination charge

construction.quote: Not later than 60 days after the effective date of the termination of a contract under this section, the service provider under the contract shall refund to the servicemember any fee or other amount to the extent paid for a period extending until after such date

atoms.reasoning: 3956(b) lists covered service contracts; (e)-(f) bar early termination charges and require refunds.
atoms.origin: register queue batch 6, section US:50 USC 3956 (new_rule, major)

atoms.condition: Deciding whether a payee rule of Regulation E (US:12CFR1005.3(a)-payee-duties) applies to a transfer to or from a tenant.
atoms.effect: It applies only where the tenant is a natural person and the account debited or credited is a checking, savings or other asset account (including a prepaid account) held primarily for personal, family or household purposes; a company tenant or a business account is outside. A 'preauthorized' transfer is one authorized in advance to recur at substantially regular intervals, so a single one-time debit of a move-out balance is not governed by 1005.10(b) or (d). A debit initiated without the tenant's actual authority is an 'unauthorized' EFT, which the tenant's bank must treat under 1005.6 and 1005.11 (the tenant's liability limits and error resolution).
atoms.quote: (k) “Preauthorized electronic fund transfer” means an electronic fund transfer authorized in advance to recur at substantially regular intervals.

construction.quote: (b)(1) “Account” means a demand deposit (checking), savings, or other consumer asset account (other than an occasional or incidental credit balance in a credit plan) held directly or indirectly by a financial institution and established primarily for personal, family, or household purposes.
(e) “Consumer” means a natural person.

atoms.reasoning: The definitions fix the reach of each payee duty: consumer, account and preauthorized transfer.
atoms.origin: register queue batch 6, section US:12 CFR 1005.2 (new_rule, minor)

atoms.actor: landlord; managing agent; Handoff; collector (as furnisher)
atoms.condition: A former tenant (or a person billed for a tenancy) gives the furnisher an identity theft report to stop it furnishing the balance (US:15USC1681c-2-furnisher-identity-theft).
atoms.effect: An identity theft report is a copy of an official report filed with a law enforcement agency (false filing being a crime) alleging identity theft as specifically as the consumer can. The furnisher may ask for additional information reasonably needed to judge validity within 15 days of receiving the report, make any supplemental request and final determination within another 15 days (5 days if the information arrives on the 11th day or later); a detailed report bearing the officer's identification is sufficient on its face without an identifiable concern, while an automated report with a bare allegation may be supplemented by the CFPB identity theft affidavit and identification.
atoms.quote: (i)(1) Identity theft report means a report: (i) That alleges identity theft with as much specificity as the consumer can provide; (ii) That is a copy of an official, valid report filed by the consumer with a Federal, state, or local law enforcement agency, including the United States Postal Inspection Service, the filing of which subjects the person filing the report to criminal penalties relating to the filing of false information, if, in fact, the information in the report is false; and

construction.quote: Makes such request not later than fifteen days after the date of receipt of the copy of the report form

atoms.reasoning: 1022.3(i)(1)(iii) sets the furnisher's windows for requesting more information; (i)(3) gives the examples.
atoms.origin: register queue batch 6, section US:12 CFR 1022.3 (new_rule, major)

atoms.condition: The landlord (or Handoff for it) offers a former tenant who is a natural person a payment plan for the move-out balance and charges, as an incident to the plan, interest, a time-price differential, a service or carrying charge, a plan set-up or similar fee, or a credit-report fee.
atoms.effect: Each such charge is a finance charge, so the plan is consumer credit 'for which the payment of a finance charge is or may be required'. A landlord that regularly offers such plans (or regularly offers plans payable in more than four installments) is a TILA creditor (US:15USC1602(g)) and each covered plan requires the TILA part B closed-end credit disclosures before consummation. Amounts that would be owed anyway in a comparable cash transaction (the rent, damage and lawful lease charges themselves) are not finance charges. A plan with no finance charge and at most four installments does not make the landlord a creditor.
judgment_terms: incident to the extension of credit
atoms.quote: the amount of the finance charge in connection with any consumer credit transaction shall be determined as the sum of all charges, payable directly or indirectly by the person to whom the credit is extended, and imposed directly or indirectly by the creditor as an incident to the extension of credit. The finance charge does not include charges of a type payable in a comparable cash transaction.

construction.quote: Interest, time price differential, and any amount payable under a point, discount, or other system or additional charges.

atoms.reasoning: 1605(a) defines the finance charge by charges imposed incident to the credit, excluding comparable cash charges; 1602(g) makes a regular extender of credit with a finance charge a creditor.
atoms.origin: register queue batch 6, section US:15 USC 1605 (new_rule, critical)

atoms.condition: The landlord sends electronically a record that law requires to be given in writing, or relies on an electronic signature (lease, autopay authorization, payment plan, settlement).
atoms.effect: The consumer-consent requirements (US:15USC7001(c)-esign-consent) apply only where the tenant is a consumer: an individual who obtains the tenancy primarily for personal, family or household purposes, or that individual's legal representative. A company tenant, or an individual renting for business use, is not; records to it may be sent electronically without the 7001(c) disclosures and consent. The lease of real property is a 'transaction', and an electronic signature is any electronic sound, symbol or process attached to or logically associated with the record and executed or adopted with intent to sign.
atoms.quote: The term “consumer” means an individual who obtains, through a transaction, products or services which are used primarily for personal, family, or household purposes, and also means the legal representative of such an individual.

construction.quote: the sale, lease, exchange, or other disposition of any interest in real property, or any combination thereof.

The term “electronic signature” means an electronic sound, symbol, or process, attached to or logically associated with a contract or other record and executed or adopted by a person with the intent to sign the record.

atoms.reasoning: 7001(c) protects a 'consumer' as 7006(1) defines it; 7006(13)(B) includes real-property leases.
atoms.origin: register queue batch 6, section US:15 USC 7006 (partial, major)

atoms.instrument: 24 CFR part 982 (Section 8 Tenant-Based Assistance: Housing Choice Voucher Program)
atoms.condition: The PHA paid the owner housing assistance for a period after the move-out month or after the HAP contract ended, or the owner otherwise breached the HAP contract (for example HQS failures).
atoms.effect: The PHA may recover the overpayment from the owner, abate or reduce payments, or terminate the contract. An overpayment is repaid to the PHA; it is not credited to or charged against the tenant's account.
atoms.quote: The PHA rights and remedies against the owner under the HAP contract include recovery of overpayments, abatement or other reduction of housing assistance payments, termination of housing assistance payments, and termination of the HAP contract.
atoms.origin: register queue batch 6, section US:24 CFR 982.453 (new_rule, major)

atoms.instrument: 24 CFR part 982 (Section 8 Tenant-Based Assistance: Housing Choice Voucher Program)
atoms.condition: A voucher family's assistance fell to zero (for example after an income increase) and 180 calendar days have passed since the last housing assistance payment to the owner.
atoms.effect: The HAP contract has ended automatically; from then on the tenancy is not a voucher tenancy, and its settlement follows state and local law alone, without the part 982 deposit and charge rules (US:24CFR982.313(c), US:24CFR982.451(b)(4)).
atoms.quote: The HAP contract terminates automatically 180 calendar days after the last housing assistance payment to the owner.
atoms.origin: register queue batch 6, section US:24 CFR 982.455 (new_rule, major)

atoms.instrument: Violence Against Women Act housing provisions, 34 U.S.C. 12491-12496
atoms.actor: landlord; managing agent; Handoff; collector (voucher owner and its agents)
atoms.condition: The unit is rented with a tenant-based voucher, and the tenant or another person has used, claimed or helped someone use VAWA housing protections, or opposed or reported a violation.
atoms.effect: The owner or manager may not discriminate against, coerce, intimidate, threaten, interfere with or retaliate against that person for it (for example by adding charges, pressing collection or reporting because the tenant invoked VAWA). HUD and the Attorney General enforce it with the rights and remedies of the Fair Housing Act (US:42USC3613-private-action, US:42USC3610-3612-hud-enforcement).
atoms.quote: No public housing agency or owner or manager of housing assisted under a covered housing program shall coerce, intimidate, threaten, or interfere with, or retaliate against, any person

construction.quote: shall implement and enforce this subpart consistent with, and in a manner that provides, the rights and remedies provided for in title VIII of the Civil Rights Act of 1968

atoms.reasoning: 12494(a)-(b) bar retaliation and coercion by owners and managers of covered housing; (c) imports the Fair Housing Act remedies.
atoms.origin: register queue batch 6, section US:34 USC 12494 (new_rule, major)

atoms.condition: Deciding whether a tenant, occupant or associate is protected as a person with a handicap (for example for an assistance-animal waiver or modification restoration at move-out) or for familial status.
atoms.effect: Handicap means a physical or mental impairment substantially limiting one or more major life activities, a record of one, or being regarded as having one; it excludes current illegal use of or addiction to a controlled substance (recovered or treated addiction and alcoholism are included). Familial status covers a household with a child under 18 living with a parent, custodian or written designee, and anyone pregnant or securing custody.
judgment_terms: substantially limits one or more major life activities
atoms.quote: but such term does not include current, illegal use of or addiction to a controlled substance (as defined in section 802 of title 21).

construction.quote: drug addiction (other than addiction caused by current, illegal use of a controlled substance) and alcoholism.

atoms.reasoning: 3602(h) and 100.201 define handicap with the drug-use exclusion; 3602(k) defines familial status.
atoms.origin: register queue batch 6, section US:42 USC 3602 (new_rule, minor)

atoms.condition: An attorney for the servicemember tenant, or a person holding the servicemember's power of attorney, gives the landlord an SCRA notice or request (for example lease termination with orders, a 6% cap request) or claims SCRA relief.
atoms.effect: The representative is treated as the servicemember, so the notice or request has the same effect as the servicemember's own. A power of attorney naming a spouse, parent or other relative, executed during service or after orders or notice of possible orders, is extended automatically while the servicemember is missing, unless its terms fix an expiry regardless of missing status.
atoms.quote: Whenever the term “servicemember” is used in this chapter, such term shall be treated as including a reference to a legal representative of the servicemember.

construction.quote: A power of attorney of a servicemember shall be automatically extended for the period the servicemember is in a missing status

atoms.reasoning: 3920(a)-(b) define the legal representative and equate it with the servicemember; 4022 keeps a qualifying power of attorney alive during missing status.
atoms.origin: register queue batch 6, section US:50 USC 3920 (new_rule, major)

atoms.condition: The tenant or former tenant pays through the landlord's or Handoff's portal by instructing each payment itself (no standing authorization), or the landlord pays a deposit refund by a prepaid card issued for that disbursement and not advertised to the public.
atoms.effect: A payment the tenant initiates each time is not a preauthorized transfer: the 1005.10(b) written-authorization and 1005.10(d) varying-amount rules do not apply to it. A refund paid on such a prepaid card is not a gift card or general-use prepaid card under 1005.20, so the gift-card fee and expiration rules do not bind the payer; the card's own account disclosures are the issuing bank's (1005.18).
atoms.quote: In contrast, if the consumer must take action each month to initiate a payment (such as by entering instructions on a touch-tone telephone or home computer), the payments are not preauthorized EFTs.

construction.quote: iv. An insurance company settles a policyholder's claim and distributes the insurance proceeds to the consumer by means of a prepaid card. Because the prepaid card is simply the means for providing the insurance proceeds to the consumer and the availability of the card is not advertised to the general public, the exclusion in § 1005.20(b)(4) applies.

atoms.reasoning: Comment 2(k)-1 limits 'preauthorized' to transfers needing no further action by the consumer; comment 20(b)(4)-2.iv excludes a prepaid card that is only the means of paying proceeds and is not marketed to the public.
atoms.origin: register queue batch 6, section US:12 CFR Supplement_I_to_Part_1005 (new_rule, minor)

atoms.instrument: Consumer Financial Protection Act of 2010, 12 U.S.C. 5481-5603
atoms.condition: The landlord (a seller of a nonfinancial service, the tenancy) gives a former tenant a payment plan or other deferral for rent or move-out charges it is owed.
atoms.effect: The CFPA does not reach that credit or the landlord's collection of it (directly or through an agent), or its sale of the plan once in default, unless: (i) the landlord assigns or sells the plan debt before default; (ii) the credit significantly exceeds the market value of the tenancy or is a subterfuge; or (iii) the landlord regularly extends credit subject to a finance charge. Even under (iii), the exclusion stands if the landlord is not significantly engaged in consumer financial products, which it is deemed not to be if it only extends credit for its own tenancies, keeps the credit on its own books (except selling defaulted debt) and is a small business under the Small Business Act size standard. Where the exclusion stands, state attorneys general also cannot bring CFPA claims about it.
atoms.quote: extends credit directly to a consumer, in a case in which the good or service being provided is not itself a consumer financial product or service (other than credit described in this subparagraph), exclusively for the purpose of enabling that consumer to purchase such nonfinancial good or service directly from the merchant, retailer, or seller;

construction.quote: in which the merchant, retailer, or seller of nonfinancial goods or services regularly extends credit and the credit is subject to a finance charge.
retains such credit on its own accounts (except to sell or convey such debt that is delinquent or otherwise in default); and

atoms.reasoning: 5517(a)(2)(A) excludes merchant credit for its own nonfinancial service; (B) lists the exceptions; (C)(i)-(ii) and (D)(ii) restore the exclusion for a small merchant-creditor; (E) bars state CFPA claims where it holds.
atoms.origin: register queue batch 6, section US:12 USC 5517 (new_rule, major)

atoms.condition: The landlord, manager or Handoff communicates information about a former tenant's tenancy, balance or payment history to someone else. Branches: (a) the landlord (or its agent) states only its own experience with the tenant, to a collector, a consumer reporting agency, or a prospective landlord; (b) Handoff, for fees, regularly assembles or evaluates tenants' settlement or payment information from several owners and provides it to third parties (for example to other owners screening applicants).
atoms.effect: (a) A report containing only the landlord's own transactions or experiences with the tenant is not a consumer report, and the landlord is not a consumer reporting agency; when it sends that information to a consumer reporting agency it is a furnisher under 1681s-2 and Regulation V subpart E. (b) Handoff is then a consumer reporting agency and every communication used for eligibility is a consumer report, with the full agency duties (permissible purpose, accuracy procedures, disclosures, disputes). Handoff settling or collecting a tenancy for one owner, and reporting that owner's account to an agency, is branch (a).
judgment_terms: regularly engages in assembling or evaluating
atoms.quote: report containing information solely as to transactions or experiences between the consumer and the person making the report;

construction.quote: The term “consumer reporting agency” means any person which, for monetary fees, dues, or on a cooperative nonprofit basis, regularly engages in whole or in part in the practice of assembling or evaluating consumer credit information or other information on consumers for the purpose of furnishing consumer reports to third parties

atoms.reasoning: 1681a(d)(2)(A)(i) excludes first-party experience reports; 1681a(f) makes a regular fee-based assembler of consumer information for third parties a consumer reporting agency. Which branch applies to Handoff is an operating choice.
atoms.origin: register queue batch 6, section US:15 USC 1681a (new_rule, critical)

atoms.condition: The landlord or its agent (Handoff, a collector, an assignee of the balance) pulls a former tenant's consumer report to review or collect the lease account, and the tenant's file carries a security freeze, or an initial, extended or active-duty fraud alert.
atoms.effect: A security freeze does not block a report pulled by the landlord, its agent or assignee, or a prospective buyer of the balance, for reviewing or collecting the account or contract. If the report shows an initial or active-duty alert, the user may not establish a payment plan or other extension of credit in the tenant's name unless it uses reasonable procedures to form a reasonable belief that it knows who is asking (and, where the tenant gave a phone number for verification, calls it or takes reasonable steps to verify); with an extended alert, it must contact the tenant in person or by the contact method in the alert first.
judgment_terms: reasonable belief that the user knows the identity
atoms.quote: for the purposes of reviewing the account or collecting the financial obligation owed for the account, contract, or negotiable instrument.

construction.quote: No prospective user of a consumer report that includes an initial fraud alert or an active duty alert in accordance with this section may establish a new credit plan or extension of credit

atoms.reasoning: 1681c-1(i)(4)(A) excepts account review and collection by the person the consumer contracted with and its agents and assignees; 1681c-1(h) limits new extensions of credit to a consumer with an alert.
atoms.origin: register queue batch 6, section US:15 USC 1681c–1 (new_rule, minor)

atoms.condition: A person claims that the tenancy (lease application, lease or payments) billed to them was made by someone who used their identity without authority, and sends the landlord a written request for the records, at any address the landlord specified.
atoms.effect: Within 30 days of the request, and after verifying identity and the claim (government ID or matching identifying information, plus, at the landlord's election, a police report and the CFPB affidavit or an acceptable affidavit of fact) unless it already has high confidence in the requester's identity, the landlord provides free copies of the application and transaction records it controls, including records kept for it by a manager or Handoff, to the victim or the law enforcement agency the victim names. It may decline in good faith if not required, if identity remains doubtful, if the request rests on a misrepresentation, or for web navigation data. Good-faith disclosure carries no civil liability; tenants cannot sue under 1681n/1681o for violations, which are enforced publicly.
atoms.quote: not later than 30 days after the date of receipt of a request from a victim in accordance with paragraph (3), and subject to verification of the identity of the victim and the claim of identity theft in accordance with paragraph (2), a business entity that has provided credit to, provided for consideration products, goods, or services to, accepted payment from, or otherwise entered into a commercial transaction for consideration with, a person who has allegedly made unauthorized use of the means of identification of the victim, shall provide a copy of application and business transaction records in the control of the business entity, whether maintained by the business entity or by another person on behalf of the business entity, evidencing any transaction alleged to be a result of identity theft to—

construction.quote: Except as provided in section 1681s of this title, sections 1681n and 1681o of this title do not apply to any violation of this subsection.

atoms.reasoning: 1681g(e)(1)-(5) set the duty, verification and grounds to decline; (e)(6)-(7) limit liability.
atoms.origin: register queue batch 6, section US:15 USC 1681g (new_rule, major)

atoms.actor: landlord; managing agent; Handoff; collector (as furnisher)
atoms.condition: The former tenant disputes the reported balance with a consumer reporting agency, and the agency sends the furnisher notice of the dispute (it must do so within 5 business days of receiving it).
atoms.effect: The furnisher's investigation and report back (US:15USC1681s-2(b)(1)) must be completed within the agency's reinvestigation period: 30 days from the agency's receipt of the dispute, extended by up to 15 days if the tenant sends the agency relevant information during the 30 days (no extension once the item is found inaccurate or unverifiable), and 45 days where the dispute follows the tenant's free annual report. If the furnisher does not verify in time, the agency deletes or modifies the item and notifies the furnisher; the item may be reinserted only if the furnisher certifies it is complete and accurate.
atoms.quote: before the end of the 30-day period beginning on the date on which the agency receives the notice of the dispute from the consumer or reseller.

construction.quote: may be extended for not more than 15 additional days if the consumer reporting agency receives information from the consumer during that 30-day period that is relevant to the reinvestigation.
Before the expiration of the 5-business-day period beginning on the date on which a consumer reporting agency receives notice of a dispute
the information may not be reinserted in the file by the consumer reporting agency unless the person who furnishes the information certifies that the information is complete and accurate.
shall be completed not later than 45 days after the date on which the request is received.

atoms.reasoning: 1681s-2(b)(2) ties the furnisher's deadline to the 1681i(a)(1) period; 1681i(a)(1)(A)-(C), (a)(2), (a)(5) and 1681j(a)(3) fix its length and the consequences.
atoms.origin: register queue batch 6, section US:15 USC 1681i (partial, critical)

atoms.condition: The landlord or anyone collecting for it has been notified under 1681c-2 that a former tenant's balance resulted from identity theft, or a debt collector collecting it for the landlord is told that information about the balance may be fraudulent or the result of identity theft.
atoms.effect: (f) No one may sell the balance, transfer it for consideration or place it for collection after the 1681c-2 notice; this binds everyone collecting it after the notice. A transfer in a merger or sale of substantially all assets, or a required repurchase by the assignor, is not barred. (g) A debt collector collecting for the landlord must tell the landlord that the information may be fraudulent or the result of identity theft, and on the consumer's request give the consumer all the information it would be entitled to if it were disputing the balance (for a lease balance, the verification items of US:12CFR1006.38(d)(2)).
atoms.quote: No person shall sell, transfer for consideration, or place for collection a debt that such person has been notified under section 1681c–2 of this title has resulted from identity theft.

construction.quote: notify the third party that the information may be fraudulent or may be the result of identity theft; and

atoms.reasoning: 1681m(f)(1)-(3) bar placement after a 1681c-2 notice with three transfer exceptions; 1681m(g) sets the collector's duties.
atoms.origin: register queue batch 6, section US:15 USC 1681m (new_rule, critical)

atoms.condition: The landlord, manager or Handoff denies a former tenant's request for a payment plan (or grants one on less favorable terms than requested), or takes another action adverse to the tenant in a transaction the tenant initiated, based in whole or in part on information in a consumer report it obtained.
atoms.effect: It must give the tenant notice of the adverse action; any numerical credit score it used with its key factors; the name, address and telephone number of the consumer reporting agency that supplied the report and a statement that the agency did not make the decision; and notice of the right to a free report from that agency within 60 days and to dispute its accuracy. Oral, written or electronic delivery is allowed, except that the credit score disclosure is written or electronic.
judgment_terms: based in whole or in part on
atoms.quote: If any person takes any adverse action with respect to any consumer that is based in whole or in part on any information contained in a consumer report, the person shall—

construction.quote: an action taken or determination that is— (I) made in connection with an application that was made by, or a transaction that was initiated by, any consumer, or in connection with a review of an account under section 1681b(a)(3)(F)(ii) of this title; and (II) adverse to the interests of the consumer.

atoms.reasoning: 1681a(k) makes a denial of requested credit (ECOA 1691(d)(6)) and any adverse determination in a consumer-initiated transaction an adverse action; a payment plan is credit (US:15USC1602(f)).
atoms.origin: register queue batch 6, section US:15 USC 1681m (new_rule, major)

atoms.condition: A landlord, manager, Handoff or collector violates the FCRA as a furnisher or user, including the 1681s-2(a) duties that tenants cannot enforce privately.
atoms.effect: The FTC may recover a civil penalty of up to $2,500 per violation (as adjusted for inflation) for a knowing violation that is a pattern or practice, but no penalty for a 1681s-2(a)(1) accuracy violation unless the person first violated an FTC injunction or order. The New York Attorney General may sue to enjoin, and on behalf of residents for their 1681n/1681o damages, for damages a 1681s-2(a) violation would cause but for 1681s-2(c), or for up to $1,000 per willful or negligent violation, plus costs and attorney's fees.
atoms.quote: in the event of a knowing violation, which constitutes a pattern or practice of violations of this subchapter, the Federal Trade Commission may commence a civil action to recover a civil penalty in a district court of the United States against any person that violates this subchapter. In such action, such person shall be liable for a civil penalty of not more than $2,500 per violation.

construction.quote: damages of not more than $1,000 for each willful or negligent violation; and
a court may not impose any civil penalty on a person for a violation of section 1681s–2(a)(1) of this title, unless the person has been enjoined

atoms.reasoning: 1681s(a)(2) sets FTC penalties with the (C) limit for accuracy violations; 1681s(c)(1)(B) gives the State damages actions, including for 1681s-2(a) violations otherwise shielded by 1681s-2(c).
atoms.origin: register queue batch 6, section US:15 USC 1681s (new_rule, major)

atoms.condition: The market-rate unit is rented with a tenant-based Housing Choice Voucher and the tenant, or an affiliated individual, is or has been a victim of domestic violence, dating violence, sexual assault or stalking.
atoms.effect: The owner may not evict or end the tenancy on the basis or as a direct result of that status. An incident of actual or threatened violence is not a serious or repeated lease violation or good cause to end the victim's tenancy. The owner keeps its authority to comply with a court order on access to or possession of property, to evict for a violation not premised on the violence (applying no more demanding standard than to other tenants), and to evict where it shows an actual and imminent threat to other tenants or staff, and then only if no lesser measure would remove the threat. Charges for the perpetrator's acts follow US:34USC12491-VAWA.
atoms.quote: may not be denied admission to, denied assistance under, terminated from participation in, or evicted from the housing on the basis or as a direct result of the fact that the applicant or tenant is or has been a victim

construction.quote: An incident of actual or threatened domestic violence, dating violence, sexual assault, or stalking shall not be construed as:

the covered housing provider must not subject the tenant, who is or has been a victim of domestic violence, dating violence, sexual assault, or stalking, or is affiliated with an individual who is or has been a victim

atoms.reasoning: 5.2005(b)-(d) state the protections and their limits; 982.310(h)(4) makes the voucher owner's terminations subject to them.
atoms.origin: register queue batch 6, section US:24 CFR 5.2005 (partial, major)

atoms.condition: A former tenant complains to HUD about a discriminatory practice in the tenancy or settlement.
atoms.effect: The complaint is timely if filed within one year after the practice occurred or ended; HUD serves the respondent within 10 days of filing, the respondent may answer within 10 days of notice, and HUD aims to finish investigating within 100 days. Remedies follow US:42USC3610-3612-hud-enforcement.
atoms.quote: An aggrieved person may, not later than one year after an alleged discriminatory housing practice has occurred or terminated, file a complaint with the Secretary alleging such discriminatory housing practice.
atoms.origin: register queue batch 6, section US:42 USC 3610 (new_rule, major)

atoms.condition: An aggrieved former tenant files a complaint with HUD over a discriminatory housing practice in the tenancy or its settlement.
atoms.effect: The complaint may be filed within one year after the practice occurred or ended; HUD serves the respondent within 10 days, and the respondent may answer within 10 days of notice. If HUD issues a charge, any party may elect within 20 days of service to have it decided in federal court (with the relief of 3613); otherwise an ALJ may award actual damages, equitable relief and a civil penalty of up to $10,000 (no prior violation), $25,000 (one prior in 5 years) or $50,000 (two or more in 7 years), as adjusted for inflation, plus attorney's fees to the prevailing party.
atoms.quote: in an amount not exceeding $10,000 if the respondent has not been adjudged to have committed any prior discriminatory housing practice;

construction.quote: An aggrieved person may, not later than one year after an alleged discriminatory housing practice has occurred or terminated, file a complaint with the Secretary
The election must be made not later than 20 days after the receipt by the electing person of service under section 3610(h) of this title

atoms.reasoning: 3610(a) sets the one-year complaint period; 3612(a), (g)(3), (o), (p) the election, ALJ relief, penalties and fees.
atoms.origin: register queue batch 6, section US:42 USC 3612 (new_rule, critical)
register apply (ADJUDICATION_QUEUE condition 1: 11 U.S.C. 362 in full)
atoms.condition: A former tenant (or the owner) is a debtor and the landlord asks whether the automatic stay still bars collecting the balance or applying the deposit.
atoms.effect: The stay of acts against property of the estate lasts until the property leaves the estate. The stay of any other act (collecting the balance, suing, applying the deposit as a setoff) lasts until the earliest of: the case is closed; the case is dismissed; or, in an individual's chapter 7 case or a chapter 11, 12 or 13 case, a discharge is granted or denied. After the stay ends, a discharged balance stays enjoined (US:11USC524(a)(2)), and one not discharged may be collected, subject to US:11USC108(c)-extension.
atoms.quote: (2) the stay of any other act under subsection (a) of this section continues until the earliest of— (A) the time the case is closed; (B) the time the case is dismissed; or (C) if the case is a case under chapter 7 of this title concerning an individual or a case under chapter 9, 11, 12, or 13 of this title, the time a discharge is granted or denied;

atoms.origin: register apply (ADJUDICATION_QUEUE condition 1: 11 U.S.C. 362 in full)
atoms.condition: A former tenant who is an individual files a chapter 7, 11 or 13 case after one or more of its cases was dismissed within the preceding year (other than a case refiled under another chapter after a 707(b) dismissal).
atoms.effect: (a) One prior case dismissed within the year: the stay as to actions on a debt or lease terminates with respect to the debtor on the 30th day after the later filing, unless the court extends it on a motion heard within those 30 days on a showing that the later case was filed in good faith. (b) Two or more prior cases dismissed within the year: no stay arises on the filing; on the landlord's request the court promptly confirms that no stay is in effect; a party may ask within 30 days for a stay to take effect, which the court grants only on a showing of good faith, effective from its order. The landlord checks the tenant's filing history before treating a new filing as staying collection.
atoms.quote: (4) (A) (i) if a single or joint case is filed by or against a debtor who is an individual under this title, and if 2 or more single or joint cases of the debtor were pending within the previous year but were dismissed, other than a case refiled under a chapter other than chapter 7 after dismissal under section 707(b), the stay under subsection (a) shall not go into effect upon the filing of the later case; and (ii) on request of a party in interest, the court shall promptly enter an order confirming that no stay is in effect;

construction.quote: the stay under subsection (a) with respect to any action taken with respect to a debt or property securing such debt or with respect to any lease shall terminate with respect to the debtor on the 30th day after the filing of the later case;

atoms.reasoning: Section 362(c)(3) ends the stay after 30 days for a debtor with one dismissal in the prior year, and 362(c)(4) prevents the stay from arising after two or more; both allow the stay only on a showing of good faith.

atoms.origin: register apply (ADJUDICATION_QUEUE condition 1: 11 U.S.C. 362 in full)
atoms.condition: The landlord moves for relief from the stay (for example to apply the held deposit, US:FRBP4001-stay-relief-procedure).
atoms.effect: Thirty days after the request for relief from the stay of an act against property of the estate, the stay terminates as to the landlord unless the court, after notice and a hearing, continues it pending a final hearing; a preliminary hearing's final hearing must end within 30 days after it. In an individual's chapter 7, 11 or 13 case the stay terminates 60 days after the request unless the court decides within that time or the period is extended by agreement or for good cause.
atoms.quote: (e) (1) Thirty days after a request under subsection (d) of this section for relief from the stay of any act against property of the estate under subsection (a) of this section, such stay is terminated with respect to the party in interest making such request, unless the court, after notice and a hearing, orders such stay continued in effect pending the conclusion of, or as a result of, a final hearing and determination under subsection (d) of this section.

construction.quote: the stay under subsection (a) shall terminate on the date that is 60 days after a request is made by a party in interest under subsection (d), unless— (A) a final decision is rendered by the court during the 60-day period beginning on the date of the request;

atoms.reasoning: Section 362(e)(1) and (2) set the automatic termination of the stay after a relief request.

atoms.origin: register apply (ADJUDICATION_QUEUE condition 1: 11 U.S.C. 362 in full)
atoms.condition: The landlord, its manager, Handoff or a collector acts to collect a pre-petition balance, applies the deposit, or otherwise violates the stay after the tenant (an individual) filed, with notice of the case.
atoms.effect: The tenant recovers its actual damages, including costs and attorney's fees, and punitive damages in appropriate circumstances. Where the act was taken in the good-faith belief that 362(h) applies (the stay ended for failure to state intentions about property securing a debt), recovery is limited to actual damages. No monetary penalty runs for conduct before the landlord received notice effective under US:11USC342-effective-notice.
atoms.quote: (k) (1) Except as provided in paragraph (2), an individual injured by any willful violation of a stay provided by this section shall recover actual damages, including costs and attorneys’ fees, and, in appropriate circumstances, may recover punitive damages.

atoms.condition: The landlord (or Handoff arranging it for the landlord) is a TILA creditor because it regularly offers payment plans with a finance charge or payable in more than four installments (US:15USC1602(g), US:15USC1605-plan-finance-charge), and it gives a former tenant who is a natural person a closed-end payment plan for a move-out balance that US:15USC1603-plan-exemptions does not exempt.
atoms.effect: The landlord gives the tenant the part B disclosures (US:15USC1638-closed-end-disclosures). Where several people are obligated on the plan (co-tenants, a guarantor), disclosure to one primary obligor suffices. Where more than one creditor takes part, only one discloses, as Regulation Z assigns.
atoms.quote: Subject to subsection (b), a creditor or lessor shall disclose to the person who is obligated on a consumer lease or a consumer credit transaction the information required under this subchapter.
atoms.origin: register batch 9 (adjudication scope addition), section US:15 USC 1631 (new_rule, major)

atoms.condition: The landlord gives the part B disclosures for a payment plan (US:15USC1631-plan-disclosure-duty).
atoms.effect: The disclosures are clear and conspicuous; the terms 'annual percentage rate' and 'finance charge' are more conspicuous than any other term or information except the creditor's identity. The landlord may add explanations, but not within the segregated disclosures (US:15USC1638-closed-end-disclosures).
atoms.quote: The terms “annual percentage rate” and “finance charge” shall be disclosed more conspicuously than other terms, data, or information provided in connection with a transaction, except information relating to the identify of the creditor.
atoms.origin: register batch 9 (adjudication scope addition), section US:15 USC 1632 (new_rule, minor)

atoms.condition: The landlord (or Handoff arranging it for the landlord) is a TILA creditor because it regularly offers payment plans with a finance charge or payable in more than four installments (US:15USC1602(g), US:15USC1605-plan-finance-charge), and it gives a former tenant who is a natural person a closed-end payment plan for a move-out balance that US:15USC1603-plan-exemptions does not exempt.
atoms.effect: Before the plan is entered into, the landlord discloses, segregated from all other terms: its identity; the amount financed (the balance the tenant is given time to pay), with the tenant's right to a written itemization on request; the finance charge; the annual percentage rate (not required where the amount financed is $75 or less and the finance charge $5 or less, or the amount financed is over $75 and the finance charge $7.50 or less); the total of payments; the number, amounts and due dates of the payments; any late payment charge; whether a rebate of a precomputed finance charge or a prepayment penalty applies; any security interest taken; and a reference to the plan document for default, acceleration and prepayment terms. A plan entered into without these disclosures exposes the landlord under US:15USC1640-tila-civil-liability.
atoms.quote: (1) Except as otherwise provided in this part, the disclosures required under subsection (a) shall be made before the credit is extended.

construction.quote: (3) The “finance charge”, not itemized, using that term. (4) The finance charge expressed as an “annual percentage rate”, using that term.

atoms.reasoning: Section 1638(a) lists the items for credit other than an open-end plan, 'to the extent applicable'; a fixed payment plan for a set balance is closed-end credit. Section 1638(b)(1) fixes the timing (before credit is extended) and the segregation.
atoms.origin: register batch 9 (adjudication scope addition), section US:15 USC 1638 (new_rule, critical)

atoms.condition: A landlord that is a TILA creditor fails a part B requirement in a payment plan with a former tenant (missing, late or inaccurate disclosures).
atoms.effect: It is liable to the tenant for actual damages plus, in an individual action on a closed-end plan not secured by real property, twice the finance charge, not less than $200 nor more than $2,000; in a class action what the court allows, up to the lesser of $1,000,000 or 1% of the creditor's net worth; plus costs and a reasonable attorney's fee. Several failures on one plan give one recovery. The action is brought within one year of the violation, but after that year the tenant may still assert the violation by recoupment or set-off when the landlord sues on the plan. No liability for a violation the landlord proves was unintentional and a bona fide error (clerical, calculation, computer) despite procedures reasonably adapted to avoid it; an error of legal judgment is not a bona fide error; nor for acts in good-faith conformity with a Bureau rule or interpretation.
atoms.quote: (i) in the case of an individual action twice the amount of any finance charge in connection with the transaction,

construction.quote: except that the liability under this subparagraph shall not be less than $200 nor greater than $2,000,

This subsection does not bar a person from asserting a violation of this subchapter in an action to collect the debt which was brought more than one year from the date of the occurrence of the violation as a matter of defense by recoupment or set-off in such action, except as otherwise provided by State law.
an error of legal judgment with respect to a person’s obligations under this subchapter is not a bona fide error.
hold that the 1995 amendment left unaltered the $100/$1,000 limits prescribed from the start for TILA violations involving personal-property loans.

atoms.reasoning: Koons Buick v Nigh (2004) holds that the floor and ceiling stated at the end of 1640(a)(2)(A)(ii) bound clause (i) as well; the current text sets them at $200 and $2,000. New York law does not bar recoupment of the violation in the landlord's suit.
atoms.origin: register batch 9 (adjudication scope addition), section US:15 USC 1640 (new_rule, critical)

atoms.actor: buyer or assignee of a payment plan (debt buyer, Handoff owning balances)
atoms.condition: The landlord sells or assigns a TILA-covered payment plan with a former tenant (US:15USC1638-closed-end-disclosures) and the tenant sues the assignee over the disclosures.
atoms.effect: The assignee answers for a disclosure violation only if it is apparent on the face of the disclosure statement (incomplete, inaccurate or missing required terms on its face), unless the assignment was involuntary. The tenant's signed acknowledgment of receipt is conclusive proof of delivery for a later assignee without contrary knowledge. The tenant keeps its full claims against the landlord.
atoms.quote: may be maintained against any assignee of such creditor only if the violation for which such action or proceeding is brought is apparent on the face of the disclosure statement, except where the assignment was involuntary.
atoms.origin: register batch 9 (adjudication scope addition), section US:15 USC 1641 (new_rule, minor)

atoms.condition: The landlord, manager, Handoff or a collector keeps, for a business purpose, consumer information about a tenant (a consumer report, such as the move-in screening report, or any record derived from one) and discards it, or sells, donates or transfers the equipment or media that store it (for example when a tenancy file is closed).
atoms.effect: It disposes of the information by reasonable measures to protect against unauthorized access or use: policies it follows and monitors for burning, pulverizing or shredding papers, or destroying or erasing electronic media, so the information cannot practicably be read or reconstructed; or a contract, after due diligence, with a record-destruction business it monitors. A service provider holding the information for the landlord follows the same measures. Aggregate data that identifies no one is outside the rule. The rule creates no duty to keep or destroy records that other law does not impose. State disposal law does not govern this conduct (US:15USC1681t(b)(1)(F)-furnisher-preemption); the rest of the file follows NY:GBL-399-h-disposal.
judgment_terms: reasonable measures to protect against unauthorized access or use
atoms.quote: (a) Standard. Any person who maintains or otherwise possesses consumer information for a business purpose must properly dispose of such information by taking reasonable measures to protect against unauthorized access to or use of the information in connection with its disposal.

construction.quote: (b) “Consumer information” means any record about an individual, whether in paper, electronic, or other form, that is a consumer report or is derived from a consumer report.

atoms.reasoning: 15 U.S.C. 1681w directs the FTC's rule for non-bank persons; 682.2(b) reaches any person under FTC jurisdiction that possesses consumer information for a business purpose, which includes landlords, managers and collectors.
atoms.origin: register batch 9 (adjudication scope addition), section US:16 CFR 682.3 (new_rule, major)

atoms.instrument: Internal Revenue Code, information returns (26 U.S.C. ch. 61 subch. A pt. III)
atoms.actor: landlord; manager; Handoff (whoever receives the cash in its business)
atoms.condition: In the course of its business the landlord, its manager or Handoff receives more than $10,000 in cash from a former tenant or someone paying for it (for example a move-out balance or arrears paid in currency), in one transaction or in related transactions (any within 24 hours, or a series the recipient knows or has reason to know is connected).
atoms.effect: The recipient files Form 8300 stating the payer's name, address and TIN, the amount, and the date and nature of the transaction, by the 15th day after the cash is received (for installments, once the payments received within 12 months exceed $10,000), and furnishes the payer a written statement by January 31 of the next year. Cash means currency, including foreign currency and digital assets; a personal check drawn on the payer's own bank account is not cash; a cashier's check, bank draft, traveler's check or money order of $10,000 or less counts only in a designated reporting transaction (a retail sale of consumer durables, collectibles or travel, which rent is not) or where the recipient knows it is being used to avoid reporting. No one may structure payments to avoid the return.
judgment_terms: related transactions (a series the recipient knows or has reason to know is connected)
atoms.quote: (2) who, in the course of such trade or business, receives more than $10,000 in cash in 1 transaction (or 2 or more related transactions), shall make the return described in subsection (b) with respect to such transaction (or related transactions) at such time as the Secretary may by regulations prescribe.

construction.quote: The reports required by this section must be filed in accordance with the Form 8300 instructions and related publications by the 15th day after the date the cash is received.
The term related transactions means any transaction conducted between a payer (or its agent) and a recipient of cash in a 24-hour period.

atoms.reasoning: Section 6050I(a) and (e) set the duty and the payer statement; 26 CFR 1.6050I-1 sets the 15-day filing time, the related-transaction and installment rules, and the definition of cash, whose monetary-instrument branch reaches only designated reporting transactions (retail sales of consumer durables, collectibles and travel or entertainment).
atoms.origin: register batch 9 (adjudication scope addition), section US:26 USC 6050I (new_rule, major)

atoms.instrument: Internal Revenue Code, information returns (26 U.S.C. ch. 61 subch. A pt. III)
atoms.actor: payment settlement entity; Handoff or a manager by configuration
atoms.condition: A former tenant pays rent or a balance by payment card or through a third party payment network (a payment app or platform), and the payment is settled for the owner. Configuration (a): the settlement goes directly to the owner's merchant or network account (or the manager's account for that one owner). Configuration (b): Handoff (or a manager) receives settlements for several owners through one account and distributes them to the owners. Configuration (c): Handoff contracts with the settlement entity to make the settlement payments on its behalf (electronic payment facilitator).
atoms.effect: (a) The merchant acquiring bank (cards) or the third party settlement organization (networks) files Form 1099-K for the owner; the landlord files no information return on those payments, and they are not reported as rent on Form 1099-MISC (US:26CFR1.6041-1-agent-reports-rent). (b) Handoff (or the manager) is an aggregated payee: it is the participating payee toward the settlement entity and the payment settlement entity toward each owner it pays, so it files Form 1099-K for each owner for the calendar year and furnishes each owner a statement by January 31; for card payments with no minimum, for network payments only where an owner's payments exceed $20,000 and 200 transactions. (c) Handoff files the return in place of the settlement entity. Which configuration applies is an operating choice.
atoms.quote: (ii) such intermediary shall be treated as the payment settlement entity with respect to the settlement of such transactions with the participating payees.

construction.quote: (1) the amount which would otherwise be reported under subsection (a)(2) with respect to such transactions exceeds $20,000, and (2) the aggregate number of such transactions exceeds 200.

If a person receives payments from a payment settlement entity (as defined in paragraph (a)(4) of this section) on behalf of one or more participating payees and distributes such payments to one or more participating payees (as defined in paragraph (a)(5) of this section), the person is treated as: (i) The participating payee with respect to the payment settlement entity; and (ii) The payment settlement entity with respect to the participating payees to whom the person distributes payments.

atoms.reasoning: Section 6050W(b)(4)(A) makes an intermediary that settles several payees' transactions both the payee and the settlement entity; (b)(4)(B) shifts the return to an electronic payment facilitator; (e) limits third-party-network reporting to over $20,000 and 200 transactions; (f) sets the January 31 statement.
atoms.origin: register batch 9 (adjudication scope addition), section US:26 USC 6050W (new_rule, major)

atoms.instrument: Internal Revenue Code, information returns (26 U.S.C. ch. 61 subch. A pt. III)
atoms.actor: landlord (payor in its trade or business)
atoms.condition: In its trade or business the landlord pays $600 or more in a calendar year to an attorney in connection with legal services, for example a settlement or judgment on a former tenant's deposit claim paid to the tenant's attorney or by a check payable jointly to the tenant and the attorney.
atoms.effect: The landlord files an information return (Form 1099-MISC, gross proceeds paid to an attorney) for the attorney for the whole amount paid and furnishes the attorney a statement, unless the payment is the attorney's own fee for services to the landlord (reported under 6041) or another listed exception applies. The part of the payment that is income to the tenant is reported for the tenant under 6041 when it reaches the 6041 threshold (US:26CFR1.6041-1-agent-reports-rent sets it: $2,000 for payments after 2025): returning the tenant's own deposit is not income (US:26CFR1.166-1(e)-bad-debt), while damages above it, including the punitive part of a twice-the-deposit award, are gross income of the tenant.
atoms.quote: (A) In general This subsection shall apply to any payment to an attorney in connection with legal services (whether or not such services are performed for the payor).

construction.quote: makes payments aggregating $600 or more during a calendar year to an attorney in connection with legal services (whether or not the services are performed for the payor) must file an information return for such payments.
The mere fact that the payments were extracted from the wrongdoers as punishment for unlawful conduct cannot detract from their character as taxable income to the recipients.

atoms.reasoning: Section 6045(f) and 26 CFR 1.6045-5 require the attorney return at $600; the regulation's examples require a separate 6041 return for the claimant where the payment is the claimant's income. Punitive and statutory damages are gross income (Commissioner v Glenshaw Glass, 1955; 26 U.S.C. 61(a)); the return of the tenant's own trust money is not.
atoms.origin: register batch 9 (adjudication scope addition), section US:26 USC 6045 (new_rule, major)

coverage.method_note: Federal overlays were read for the chain notice/vacate -> deposit and interest -> charges and credits -> itemized statement -> refund method and payee -> balance owed -> pursue, hand off or write off. Sources were saved mechanically on 2026-09-28: statutes from uscode.house.gov (text in effect 2026-09-27), regulations from the eCFR renderer API (current), HUD handbook and model lease from hud.gov PDFs, cases from supremecourt.gov and CourtListener, the SCRA rent threshold from federalregister.gov. Every quote is checked verbatim by stage_a_check.py. Reused from the Virginia pass: US_15USC_1692a.txt, US_24CFR_966.4.txt, US_24CFR_982.313.txt, US_50USC_3955.txt. Checks run: a one-word mutation in three quotes makes stage_a_check fail; the 1692a(2), (3), (5) quotes also appear in NYC_ADC_20-489 and NYC_RCNY6_5-76, which copy the federal definitions (same text, not a misattribution); no other US quote appears in a non-US source. Resolution pass (2026-09-28): every bounded unknown was resolved into atoms with 'construction' quotes cut mechanically from saved files; files from other sites are saved with a US_ prefix (US_x* for State texts read for federal questions). USDA HB-2-3560 ch. 4 is saved from a mirror because rd.usda.gov returned HTTP 403; Wilson and Vincent texts were capped at about 50,000 characters by the extractor, and the quoted passages lie inside the saved part.

findings_that_correct_siblings: SCRA 3955 contains no security-deposit refund duty or deadline. The deposit is returned under state law; 3955(f) covers only rent paid in advance (30 days from the effective termination date), and 3955(h) makes it a crime to hold the deposit for rent accruing after termination.

NYC 6 RCNY 5-77(f)(1) cites 15 U.S.C. 1602(f); in the current Code 1602(f) defines 'credit' and 1602(g) defines 'creditor'. A landlord is a TILA creditor only if it regularly extends consumer credit payable in more than four installments or with a finance charge.

Regulation F 1006.1(c)(2): a residential-lease balance is not debt related to a consumer financial product or service (12 U.S.C. 5481(15)(A)(ii)), so the CFPB-website statement and itemization-date creditor are optional on validation notices for these balances.
